title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the road, the apostrophe and the words

questions.prompt: Three of these four sentences put the apostrophe in the wrong place. Which one is correct English?

options.text: My two sisters' cars were outside all night.
My two sister's cars were outside all night.
The childrens' coats were still in the car.
The drivers's windows were all open.

questions.explanation: "My two sisters' cars were outside all night." is the correct one: the word two puts several owners in the sentence, sisters is a plural that already ends in s, and the apostrophe simply follows that s. "My two sister's cars were outside all night." places the apostrophe in front of the s and hands the cars to one sister only, which the word two forbids. "The drivers's windows were all open." hangs a second s on a plural that carries one already. And "The childrens' coats were still in the car." is built on childrens, a form English never makes: the plural is children, so the genitive is children's.

questions.prompt: Read this line of a narration: "She gathered up her belongings, drove home along the empty road and kept her eyes on the mirror." Which list names the infinitive of every irregular verb of that line, and of no other?

options.text: to gather and to keep
to gather, to drive and to keep
to drive and to keep
to drive, to keep and to say

questions.explanation: "to drive and to keep" is the list: drove is the simple past of to drive, kept the simple past of to keep, and neither form is built with -ed. gathered is regular, gather plus -ed, so to gather belongs on no list of irregular verbs, which rules out "to gather and to keep" and "to gather, to drive and to keep". "to drive, to keep and to say" adds one verb too many: to say is irregular indeed, but its past form said is nowhere in that line. Read the line first, then sort what you find in it.

questions.prompt: Put these three moments of the story in the order in which they happen: (1) the telephone rings inside her car; (2) the other car brakes and settles behind her; (3) she kisses her husband goodnight at the centre.
questions.explanation: "3, 2, 1" is the order: the visit comes first, since she is driving home from it; the strange car appears on the road; and the telephone rings last, when the fear is at its highest. "1, 2, 3" reads the three numbers as they are printed instead of following the story. "2, 3, 1" opens on the road and only then goes back to the goodbye at the centre, but she can only be followed once she has left it. "3, 1, 2" keeps the goodbye first, then rings the telephone before the car has even appeared, so the frightening drive would have no cause left.

questions.prompt: The narrator telephones her son and Samantha answers: "He isn't home." Which fact does that reply add to the story?

options.text: Kingston left his wife a few weeks before that night.
Kingston was out of the house at that moment.
Samantha did not want to speak to the narrator.
Donald came back from the centre that evening.

questions.explanation: "Kingston was out of the house at that moment." is exactly what the three words say, no more: he is not there when his mother calls. "Kingston left his wife a few weeks before that night." turns an absence of one evening into a separation. "Samantha did not want to speak to the narrator." contradicts the fact that she picks the telephone up, and "Donald came back from the centre that evening." is impossible, since the narrator has just left him there.

questions.prompt: Read: "What we need before the exam is a quiet week." Which analysis of the word what is right?

options.text: It is an interrogative word, and the sentence asks for a fact.
It means the thing that, and the sentence insists on a point.
It is an exclamation word, and the sentence shows surprise.
It means the thing that, and the sentence makes a suggestion.

questions.explanation: "It means the thing that, and the sentence insists on a point." is the right analysis: say the thing that we need before the exam is a quiet week and the sense holds, and the frame what + subject + verb + is exists precisely to put one point forward. The sentence ends with a full stop and asks for nothing, so what is neither an interrogative nor an exclamation word there. And a suggestion would open with what about and a noun or an -ing verb, not with this frame.

questions.prompt: In which of these four situations does the word relieved describe what you feel?

options.text: Your keys were lost and you have just found them.
You are waiting for the results and you cannot sleep.
A door bangs behind you in an empty corridor.
You have never seen so much snow before.

questions.explanation: "Your keys were lost and you have just found them." is the situation: you are relieved once what you were afraid of proves not to exist, and the weight you were carrying goes. "You are waiting for the results and you cannot sleep." is worried, because the fear is still in front of you. "A door bangs behind you in an empty corridor." is where a fear begins, not where it ends, and "You have never seen so much snow before." is very surprised. Nothing is relieved until something has first been feared.
